notes: The whole 82-page PDF, read end to end: the preface, the national and local Progressive movement, the Progressive Era architecture introduction, and all ten style themes — Beaux Arts Classicism, Chicago School, Mission Revival, Early 20th Century American Commercial, Classical Revival, Tudor Revival, Colonial Revival, Dutch Colonial Revival, Georgian Revival and Craftsman — each with its narrative, evaluation criteria, eligibility standards, character-defining features, integrity considerations and figures, plus the bibliography. Same shape as the Victorian Era Styles statement and by the same team: no inventory table, no APN, and the yield is the figure captions and the narrative lists of known examples. Denser than the Victorian one because it names an architect or builder for most of what it illustrates.

coverage.remaining: None. The document was read in full; nothing in it is outstanding.
coverage.note: 69 numbered-address mentions across 82 pages. Two buildings are addressed on both their streets and so carry two findings each — the Ellinwood Residence at 2799 Pacific Avenue and 2498 Divisadero Street, and the Doolan/Larson Residence and Storefronts at 557 Ashbury Street and 1500-1512 Haight Street — and one printed range, 3917-3929 California Street, is a row of five separate houses recorded as its two printed numbers. Three buildings the document illustrates carry no usable address: the United States Post Office and Courthouse, located only as '7th and Mission Streets' and kept as a finding with no street number so the record is not read again; Building 106 in the Presidio; and the 1936 Golden Gate Investment Company residence of Fig. 44, captioned without an address at all. The last two are not recorded. Two figure captions name a past resident; under 'People are the hard limit' neither was extracted.
